title: Part 1
text: Imagine a fish with no jaw and no side fins, locked inside a box of bone. This one lived, and the fossils show how.

title: Part 2
text: Sacabambaspis was a jawless fish about twenty-five centimeters long, and it swam in Ordovician seas roughly 450 million years ago.
nxt: It belongs to a group called the jawless fishes. Instead of upper and lower jaws that bite, its mouth was a simple opening, surrounded by small plates.

text: It could not tear flesh from prey, and it could not bite to defend itself.

nxt: Many scientists think it fed by taking in small bits of food from the water or the sea floor, but we do not have a fossil of a meal to prove it.

title: Part 3
text: Then there are the fins. Modern fish and sharks have paired fins on their sides. They work like small wings, helping the fish steer, roll, and brake.
nxt: Sacabambaspis had no paired fins at all, no pectoral fins and no pelvic fins. Imagine trying to steer through open water without rudders.

nxt: Sharp turns and hovering in place would have been very hard for this animal.

title: Part 4
text: So how did it move? Almost all of its power would have come from its tail, which was flattened and ended in a fin.
nxt: By swinging its tail from side to side, it pushed itself forward. The front half of its body was covered in bony armor, so the head could not bend.

title: Part 5
text: The armor made another problem. Bone is heavy.
nxt: A fish with no swim bladder, the gas-filled organ that many modern fish use to float, may have had to keep swimming to stay off the bottom.

nxt: Many scientists think Sacabambaspis lived close to the sea floor, but this is an interpretation based on its body shape, not something we can see in the rock.

title: Part 6
text: A fish like this looks like a poor design. But it was not alone.
nxt: Close relatives with the same kind of armor are known from other parts of the world, so this body plan worked.

nxt: Being slow and armored was one way to live in a sea full of larger animals.

title: Part 7
text: And it matters for us. Our own ancestors did not have jaws at first. Jaws came later, when parts of the gill supports were reshaped into hinged jaws.
nxt: Evolution had to start somewhere, and it started with fish like this.
